source_text: Igitur si neque ut impossibilem neque ut periculosam deo repudias corporationem, superest ut quasi indignam reicias et accuses. Ab ipsa quidem exorsus nativitate, perora, age, iam spurcitias genitalium in utero elementorum, humoris et sanguinis foeda coagula, carnis ex eodem coeno alendae per novem menses. Describe uterum de die insolescentem, gravem, anxium, nec somno tutum, incertum lihidinibus fastidii et gulae. Invehere iam et in ipsum mulieris enitentis pudorem, vel pro periculo honorandum, vel pro natura religiosum. Horres utique et infantem cum suis impedimentis profusum, utique et ablutum dedignaris, quod pannis dirigitur, quod unctionibus formatur, quod blanditiis deridetur. Hanc venerationem naturae, Marcion, despuis, et quomodo natus es? odisti nascentem hominem, et quomodo diligis aliquem? Te quidem plane non amasti, cum ab ecclesia et fide Christi recessisti. Sed videris, si tibi displices, aut si aliter es natus. Certe Christus dilexit hominem illum in immunditiis in utero coagulatum, illum per pudenda prolatum, illum per ludibria nutritum. Propter eum descendit, propter eum praedicavit, propter eum omni se humilitate deiecit usque ad mortem, et mortem crucis; amavit utique quem magno redemit. Si Christus creatoris est, suum merito amavit; ai ab alio deo est, magis adamavit, quando alienum redemit. Amavit ergo cum homine etiam nativitatem, etiam carnem eius. Nihil amari potest sine eo per quod est id quod est. Aut aufer nativitatem, et exhibe hominem, aut adime carnem, et praesta quem deus redemit, si haec sunt homo, quem deus redemit. Tu haec erubescenda illi facis, quem redemit, et indigna, quae nisi dilexisset non redemisset? Nativitatem reformat a morte regeneratione caelesti, carnem ab omni vexatione restituit, leprosam emaculat, caecam reluminat, paralyticam redintegrat, daemoniacam expiat, mortuam resuscitat, et nos illam erubescemus? Si revera de lupa aut sue aut vacca prodire voluisset et ferae aut pecoris corpore indutus regnum caelorum praedicaret, tua, opinor, illi censura praescriberet, Turpe hoc deo, et indignum hoc dei filio, et stultum. Propterea quia ita credat; si plane stultum si de nostro sensu iudicemus deum. Sed circumspice, Marcion, si tamen non delesti: Stulta mundi elegit deus, ut confundat sapientia. Quaenam haec stulta sunt? Conversio hominum ad culturam veri dei, reiectio erroris, disciplina iustitiae, pudicitiae, misericordiae, patientiae, innocentiae omnis? Haec quidem stulta non sunt. Quaere ergo de quibus dixerit; et si praesumpseris invenisse, num erit tam stultum quam credere in deum natum, et quidem ex virgine, et quidem carneum, qui per illas naturae contumelias volutatus sit? Dicat haec aliquis stulta non esse, et alia sint quae deus in aemulationem elegerit sapientiae saecularis. Et tamen apud illam facilius creditur Iuppiter taurus factus aut cygnus quam vere homo Christus penes Marcionem.
thought_title: If birth is not impossible or dangerous for God, Marcion must still call it shameful—but Christ loved the very man born in filth and redeemed him
orientation: Tertullian is addressing Marcion directly, pressing the objection that the incarnation is unworthy of God after having already set aside the claims that it was impossible or dangerous.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore if you do not reject the taking of a body as impossible for God nor as dangerous, it remains that you reject and accuse it as unworthy. Having begun indeed from birth itself, plead on, come now, against the filths of the genital elements in the womb, the foul clots of moisture and blood, the flesh to be nourished from the same mire through nine months. Describe the womb growing insolent day by day, heavy, anxious, not safe even in sleep, uncertain in the desires of disgust and appetite. Inveigh now also against the very modesty of the woman giving birth, which is to be honored either because of the danger or reverenced because of nature. You shudder of course also at the infant poured forth with its own hindrances, of course you disdain it also when washed, because it is straightened by swaddling cloths, because it is shaped by anointings, because it is mocked by caresses. This veneration of nature, Marcion, you spit upon, and how were you born? You hate the man being born, and how do you love anyone? Yourself indeed you plainly did not love, when you withdrew from the church and the faith of Christ. But it is your concern, if you displease yourself, or if you were born otherwise. Certainly Christ loved that man coagulated in the uncleannesses in the womb, that man brought forth through the shameful parts, that man nourished through mockeries. For his sake he came down, for his sake he preached, for his sake he cast himself down with all humility even to death, and the death of the cross; he loved of course the man whom he redeemed at great price. If Christ is of the creator, he loved his own deservedly; but if he is from another god, he loved him more, since he redeemed another's. He loved therefore along with the man also his birth, also his flesh. Nothing can be loved without that through which it is what it is. Either take away birth, and show the man, or remove flesh, and present the man whom God redeemed, if these are the man, whom God redeemed. Do you make these things shameful for him, whom he redeemed, and unworthy, which if he had not loved he would not have redeemed? He reforms birth from death by heavenly regeneration, he restores flesh from every affliction, he cleanses the leprous flesh, he gives light again to the blind flesh, he restores the paralytic flesh, he purifies the demon-possessed flesh, he raises the dead flesh, and we are ashamed of it? If truly he had willed to come forth from a she-wolf or a sow or a cow and clothed in the body of a wild beast or a herd animal were to preach the kingdom of heaven, your judgment, I think, would prescribe to him, This is shameful for God, and this is unworthy of the Son of God, and foolish. Therefore because one believes so; if plainly foolish if we judge God from our own sense. But look around, Marcion, if however you have not erased it: God chose the foolish things of the world, to confound wisdom. What are these foolish things? The conversion of men to the worship of the true God, the rejection of error, the discipline of justice, of chastity, of mercy, of patience, of all innocence? These indeed are not foolish. Seek therefore about what things he said it; and if you will have presumed to have found it, will it be as foolish as to believe in God born, and indeed from a virgin, and indeed fleshly, who rolled about through those insults of nature? Someone may say these things are not foolish, and that there are other things which God chose in rivalry with worldly wisdom. And yet among that wisdom Jupiter is more easily believed to have become a bull or a swan than Christ to be truly man among Marcion.

choices.why: The noun refers to the act of assuming a body, not the body itself; 'taking of a body' preserves the verbal force and avoids the abstract 'incarnation' which is not in the Latin.

choices.english: the filths of the genital elements in the womb
choices.why: Keeps the plural 'filths' and the literal 'genital elements' to preserve the deliberately crude, rhetorical force of Tertullian's mock description of gestation.
rejected: the impurities of the generative elements
the filth of the genital parts

choices.english: the foul clots of moisture and blood
choices.why: Literal rendering of 'foeda coagula' as 'foul clots' preserves the medical-grotesque register Tertullian uses to caricature the objection.
rejected: the foul congealing of fluid and blood
the disgusting coagulation of moisture and blood

choices.term: carnis ex eodem coeno alendae per novem menses
choices.english: the flesh to be nourished from the same mire through nine months
choices.why: The gerundive 'alendae' expresses necessity or destiny; 'to be nourished' keeps that force, and 'mire' renders 'coeno' literally.
rejected: the flesh nourished from the same filth
the flesh fed from the same slime

choices.english: uncertain in the desires of disgust and appetite
choices.why: The reading 'lihidinibus' is likely a variant of 'libidinibus'; 'desires of disgust and appetite' preserves the paradox of craving and revulsion in pregnancy.
rejected: uncertain in the lusts of loathing and gluttony
unsettled by the cravings of disgust and appetite

choices.why: 'Ludibria' means things that provoke laughter or mockery; 'mockeries' keeps the sense that the infant's care appears ridiculous to Marcion.

pass_b_english: So if you do not reject the taking of a body as impossible for God or as dangerous for him, it remains for you to reject it as unworthy and to accuse it. Begin with birth itself, then—go on, plead your case: the filths of the genital elements in the womb, the foul clots of moisture and blood, the flesh to be nourished from the same mire through nine months. Describe the womb growing swollen day by day, heavy, anxious, not even safe in sleep, uncertain in the cravings and aversions. Attack now also the very modesty of the woman giving birth—a modesty to be honored for its danger, or to be revered for its nature. You shudder, of course, at the infant poured forth with all its burdens, and of course you scorn it once it is washed, because it is bound in swaddling cloths, because it is shaped by anointings, because it is laughed at with caresses. This veneration of nature, Marcion, you spit on—and how were you born? You hate the newborn man, and how do you love anyone? You certainly did not love yourself when you withdrew from the church and the faith of Christ. But that is your concern, if you displease yourself or if you were born otherwise. Certainly Christ loved that man coagulated in the uncleannesses of the womb, that man brought forth through the shameful parts, that man nourished through mockeries. For him he descended, for him he preached, for him he cast himself down in all humility even to death, even death on a cross. He loved, surely, the one whom he redeemed at great cost. If Christ belongs to the Creator, he loved his own, as he deserved; but if he is from another god, he loved him all the more, since he redeemed what was alien. He loved, then, along with the man, also his birth, also his flesh. Nothing can be loved without that through which it is what it is. Either take away birth and produce a man, or take away flesh and present the one whom God redeemed—if these are the man whom God redeemed. Do you make shameful and unworthy for him the very things he redeemed, which he would not have redeemed if he had not loved them? He reforms birth from death by heavenly regeneration, he restores flesh from every affliction, he cleanses the leprous, gives light again to the blind, makes the paralytic whole, purges the demon-possessed, raises the dead—and we are ashamed of that flesh? If he had truly wished to come forth from a wolf or a sow or a cow, and clothed in the body of a wild beast or a herd animal had preached the kingdom of heaven, your judgment, I suppose, would prescribe to him: This is shameful for God, and unworthy of the Son of God, and foolish. Because that is what you believe—and it would indeed be foolish if we were to judge God by our own sense. But look around, Marcion, if you have not erased it: God chose the foolish things of the world to confound wisdom. What are these foolish things? The conversion of men to the worship of the true God, the rejection of error, the discipline of justice, chastity, mercy, patience, all innocence? These are not foolish. Ask, then, what he meant; and if you presume to have found it, will it be as foolish as believing in a God who was born—and born of a virgin, and fleshly at that—who rolled about through those insults to nature? Someone may say these things are not foolish, and that there are other things which God chose to rival worldly wisdom. And yet among that wisdom it is more easily believed that Jupiter became a bull or a swan than that Christ was truly a man, according to Marcion.
notes: The word 'lihidinibus' appears to be a variant or possible corruption of 'libidinibus' (desires); the gloss renders it as 'desires'.

problems.why: 'Insolent' for pregnant womb is odd; suggests 'swollen/proud' but reads as moral failing.

problems.fix: Clarify whether this is Marcion's position or Tertullian's counter-argument.

problems.why: Marcion is called 'that man from Pontus' without explicit identification; a first-time reader may not know this is Marcion.
problems.fix: Add '(Marcion)' after 'that man from Pontus' on first use.

fixed: The glossary problems about 'the foolish things of the world', 'the necessary shame of faith', and 'flesh of course' do not correspond to any text in this section; no edit made.

The speaker problem about 'Begin with birth itself' is not a real issue: the source addresses Marcion directly ('perora, age') and then continues in the second person throughout; the English does the same.
The glossary problem about 'that man from Pontus' does not correspond to any text in this section; no edit made.
The earlier edit removing the scriptural citation was correct; the source does not cite the verse explicitly, and the brief does not require adding citations.
'Insolent' for 'insolescentem' is misleading; changed to 'swollen' to match the physical sense of the womb growing heavy and distended.
'Disgust and appetite' misrenders 'fastidii et gulae'; changed to 'cravings and aversions' to capture the pregnancy-related nausea and food desires.
The sentence about judging God by our own sense is Tertullian's own parenthetical remark, not Marcion's; added 'that is' to clarify the syntax without changing the meaning.

problems.quote: Because he would believe it so—if it is plainly foolish, that is, for us to judge God by our own sense.
problems.source_quote: Propterea quia ita credat; si plane stultum si de nostro sensu iudicemus deum.
problems.why: The subject 'he' is unclear and the sentence cannot be followed. The source gives the reason for Marcion's censure: it is foolish only if we judge God by our own sense.
problems.fix: Because that is what you believe; and it would indeed be foolish, if we were to judge God by our own sense.

fixed: Fixed unclear 'he would believe it so' against 'Propterea quia ita credat; si plane stultum si de nostro sensu iudicemus deum': generic/third-person 'credat' rendered as address to Marcion ('you believe') and second clause clarified as conditional on judging God by our own sense.

last_rejected.quote: because it is laughed at with caresses
last_rejected.why: 'deridetur' = 'is mocked/laughed at'; 'blanditiis' = 'caresses/enticements'. The infant is mocked BY caresses, not the other way around. The English reverses the sense.
last_rejected.fix: because it is mocked with caresses
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'deridetur ... blanditiis' = mocked by caresses; English 'laughed at with caresses' matches.

last_rejected.quote: Describe the womb growing insolent day by day
last_rejected.why: Latin ‘insolescentem’ means ‘growing’ or ‘increasing’, not ‘insolent’; the sense is changed.
last_rejected.fix: Describe the womb growing day by day
last_rejected.ruling: 'insolescentem' literally means 'growing insolent'; 'de die' = 'day by day'. Translation captures the rhetorical personification correctly.

last_rejected.quote: born—and born of a virgin, and fleshly at that
last_rejected.source_quote: (no corresponding passage in the Latin text)
last_rejected.why: The Latin passage does not mention a virgin birth or describe Christ as ‘fleshly’; these ideas are added.
last_rejected.fix: Remove the clause about a virgin birth and ‘fleshly’; keep the original wording about belief in a God who was born.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'et quidem ex virgine, et quidem carneum' = 'and indeed of a virgin, and indeed fleshly'. Both virgin birth and fleshly nature are in the source.

last_rejected.quote: than that Christ was truly a man, according to Marcion.
last_rejected.source_quote: quam vere homo Christus penes Marcionem.
last_rejected.why: penes Marcionem marks where true manhood is the harder belief. The English reads as if Marcion affirms that Christ was truly man.
last_rejected.fix: And yet among that wisdom, as with Marcion, it is more easily believed that Jupiter became a bull or a swan than that Christ was truly a man.
last_rejected.ruling: "penes Marcionem" = 'with/in Marcion's view'; English 'according to Marcion' conveys the same. Marcion denied true flesh, so reading matches; only slightly ambiguous placement.
